answer:
So I had a chance to interview two great CIOs recently, one from Dish Network and another from Workday (now part of Oracle), both very enterprise-focused, but with slightly different approaches.  Both were super smart and insightful.
Both thought that even if they didn’t need any new apps right now, the best ones could grow into bigger things over time. That’s how you build a career-long relationship with your vendors.
But here was what surprised me:
The CIO of Workday said he would take meetings from “any vendor” with >100 customers
. And so did the CIO of DISH network. So why wouldn’t this work well for smaller start-ups? It turns out, there are some social contracts between larger enterprises and their vendors. And those contracts can be helpful when you want to scale up later … and sometimes even today. But first let’s talk about why most CIOs don’t think much about taking meetings from tiny start-ups:
First, just because something is cool doesn’t mean we’re going to use it
. Most folks just won’t have heard of many start-ups yet, no matter how innovative they may seem. Second, we worry too much about security risks. We all know this, but it’s true again and again. CIOs and CISOs especially care deeply about risk management, which means minimizing unknown threats. Third, we tend to buy products from companies that already have our data in them
. This makes sense, since we’ve built business processes around existing systems. Fourth, we usually don’t want to learn more than 5–6 new features per year
. As you can see above, you’ll probably get that many features anyway. Fifth, we rarely like to switch vendors unless we absolutely have to.

answer: Can an 8-Person StartUp Sell to a CIO? Yes — If You Understand The Social Contract In today's complex enterprise landscape, most startups believe they can't compete with established players when selling their products to Chief Information Officers (CIOs). But what if I told you that even an eight-person company could successfully navigate this challenging environment? It’s all about understanding the social contract between vendors and buyers. The Great Expectations Framework As I’ve learned through my experience working with top-tier companies like Salesforce, Google, and Microsoft, there exists a fascinating dynamic in enterprise software sales called the “Great Expectations” framework. This concept suggests that both parties—vendors and buyers—have different expectations when engaging in business relationships. Vendors expect: • Early wins and rapid ROI realization • Low-risk implementations • Minimal investment requirements Buyers expect: • Long-term strategic partnerships • Deep integration capabilities • Proven track records of success However, here’s where things get interesting. These expectations aren’t always aligned, especially when dealing with early-stage companies. That’s why having exceptional customer success teams becomes crucial. The Customer Success Advantage Let me share a personal anecdote that illustrates this point perfectly. When I was running EchoSign, we had an incredible customer success team led by our VP of Customer Success, Karen Applegate. Her team didn’t just focus on renewals—they actively worked with customers to drive adoption and value realization. Their approach included: • Quarterly Business Review meetings to ensure alignment • Weekly check-ins to address any concerns or challenges • Collaborative roadmap planning to meet evolving needs One remarkable example stands out

answer:
So we're all here talking about how to go out there and start up your own company, get yourself into the enterprise. And I was thinking maybe it's time for me to bring back one of my favorite stories because this week I had two of my best customers, two of our biggest customers that have been with us since Day One, call me to say they'd renewed. Both are over seven figures now combined, but both started off as tiny pilots. So I thought what better way than just to share that story with you today.
I'm going to tell you why these guys were able to buy eight-person companies like ours, and then give some advice on how you can increase your odds of getting into Fortune 500 deals when you're still very small.
This is actually pretty simple if you understand social contract between buyers and sellers. This might be the most important thing to learn as a founder. It's really understanding who the buyer is, who their stakeholders are, and making sure those folks believe in you so that they'll take risk on behalf of others within the organization.
If you don't know anything else about sales, know this: buying software is a political act. Buying software is a political act, especially when you've got internal stakeholders involved. It has nothing to do with functionality per se. Don't waste your breath telling me about features and functions. Those are table stakes. It has everything to do with who believes in you. Who thinks this is a good idea. Who sees value in doing business with you.
The more people who think that, the higher you jump up the org chart.

answer:
Hey everyone,
I'm excited today to dig into an epic SaaS company called Monday.com. Now we've talked about Monday before on our podcast, our YouTube channel, and our blog quite a lot actually. We last checked in at $240 million in ARR, which was back in January of this year, and wow what a journey it's been since then.
Monday's gone from $240 million to half a billion dollars in ARR already this year. Let me take a quick look at some interesting learnings and trends that I think will be helpful to us. Number one, revenue up 91% customer count up just 34%.
The math of going upmarket. A great reminder that while it's good to add more small businesses, there are also advantages to going upmarket and targeting bigger companies. Now I personally get a little worried when this ratio falls below two to one, if only because sometimes upsell can mask lower growth in new accounts. So I want to see this ratio stay above 2:1.
But at any rate, this ratio falling from 6x to 3x as Monday goes upmarket is a big change. It's been fueled by a big increase in their $50K plus customers, who are up 200% to 793 a year ago. That's the key driver to Monday's hypergrowth as it approaches $500 million in ARR. Number two, 10-plus users sweet spot now. Again, as part of going upmarket, Monday's 10 plus seat customers are now 72% of total revenue, up from 63% just a year ago. This trend, where larger customers fuel more growth than adding more tiny ones, is something we're seeing across the board now in SaaS.
Asana, HubSpot, Shopify, Bill, Twilio. These are all seeing a massive percentage of their revenue come from 1000 or more seat customers. So maybe do the same. Maybe go more enterprise earlier if possible.
